splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), is conjunctive (requiring all three criminal-history criteria to disqualify a defendant) or disjunctive (any one criterion disqualifies).
splits.description: The circuits are deeply split on whether defendants must meet all three criminal-history criteria in § 3553(f)(1) to be disqualified from safety-valve relief, or whether possessing any one criterion is disqualifying. This affects whether district courts must impose sentences without regard to statutory minimums, with significant liberty implications for criminal defendants.

positions.label: 'And' means conjunctive — all three criteria required to disqualify
positions.summary: Holds that defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria listed in § 3553(f)(1).

positions.label: 'And' means disjunctive — any one criterion disqualifies
positions.summary: Holds that possessing any one of the three criminal-history criteria listed in § 3553(f)(1) is sufficient to disqualify a defendant from safety-valve relief.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity trumps agency or Sentencing Commission deference (Auer/Kisor deference) when interpreting ambiguous criminal sentencing provisions.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether lenity should prevail over deference to agency or Sentencing Commission interpretations in criminal contexts. At least three circuits hold lenity trumps deference, while the Third Circuit held deference trumps lenity. The issue has become more pressing after Loper Bright overruled Chevron deference.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity takes precedence over agency or Sentencing Commission deference when interpreting ambiguous criminal provisions, preventing agencies from expanding criminal liability.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that agency or Sentencing Commission deference prevails over the rule of lenity, allowing the Commission's interpretation to control even in criminal sentencing contexts.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Sentencing Guidelines' commentary (Application Note 1) can expand the definition of 'controlled substance offense' in U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2(b) to include inchoate offenses like conspiracy, when the guideline text does not mention them.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether Application Note 1 to § 4B1.2, which adds conspiracy and other inchoate offenses to the definition of 'controlled substance offense,' is a valid interpretation entitled to deference under Stinson/Kisor, or impermissibly expands the guideline's plain text. This affects career-offender designations and substantially impacts sentencing ranges.

positions.label: Commentary validly includes inchoate offenses
positions.summary: Holds that Application Note 1's inclusion of inchoate offenses like conspiracy is entitled to deference as a reasonable interpretation of the ambiguous guideline text.

positions.label: Commentary impermissibly expands guideline text
positions.summary: Holds that the guideline text unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses and that the commentary cannot add to or expand the guideline's substantive scope, particularly after Kisor narrowed deference to agency interpretations.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a non-retroactive change in sentencing law (such as the First Step Act's anti-stacking amendment to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c)) can constitute an 'extraordinary and compelling reason' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether courts may consider non-retroactive changes in law as contributing to extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release. The Seventh and Eighth Circuits hold that non-retroactive changes cannot contribute, while other circuits permit courts to consider them. The Sentencing Commission's 2024 policy statement (§ 1B1.13(b)(6)) attempted to resolve this but some circuits question its authority.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes cannot support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that a non-retroactive change in law, whether alone or combined with other factors, cannot constitute or contribute to 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' for sentence reduction under § 3582(c)(1)(A).

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes may support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that courts may consider non-retroactive changes in law as a factor contributing to extraordinary and compelling reasons for sentence reduction, particularly for defendants serving unusually long sentences.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether district courts may expressly impose revocation sentences to punish defendants for violations of supervised release, rather than solely to facilitate reentry and protect the public.
splits.description: The Sixth Circuit permits district courts to punish defendants for supervised release violations, placing it at the extreme of a circuit split. Other circuits hold that revocation sentences should serve the statutory purposes of deterrence and public protection rather than retribution. This affects hundreds of individuals facing revocations annually.

positions.label: Punishment is permissible
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may expressly impose revocation sentences to punish defendants for violations of supervised release terms.

positions.label: Punishment is not a permissible purpose
positions.summary: Holds that supervised release revocation sentences should serve reentry and public protection purposes, not punish the defendant for the violation itself, consistent with the statutory framework of 18 U.S.C. § 3583(e).

splits.legalQuestion: Whether federal prisoners challenging the conditions (rather than the fact or duration) of their confinement may proceed via habeas corpus under 28 U.S.C. § 2241, or whether they must use a civil rights action (e.g., Bivens).
splits.description: Since Preiser v. Rodriguez, a longstanding circuit split has developed over whether habeas corpus is available to challenge conditions of confinement or is limited to challenges to the fact or duration of imprisonment. This affects federal prisoners seeking relief for statutory violations like First Step Act time-credit decisions. The split has persisted for over half a century without Supreme Court resolution.

positions.label: Habeas available for conditions claims
positions.summary: Holds that habeas corpus under § 2241 may be used to challenge conditions of confinement, particularly when a prisoner seeks a change affecting the timing or manner of release such as transfer to prerelease custody.

positions.label: Habeas limited to fact/duration of confinement
positions.summary: Holds that habeas corpus is the exclusive remedy only for challenges to the fact or duration of confinement; conditions-of-confinement claims must be brought through civil rights actions.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the appeal deadline for a Hyde Amendment order (attorney's fees in criminal cases) is governed by the 30-day civil deadline or the 14-day criminal deadline under the Federal Rules of Appellate Procedure.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case (triggering a 30-day appeal deadline) or part of the criminal case (triggering a 14-day deadline). The Seventh Circuit joined the majority view that the civil deadline applies, but acknowledged a lopsided circuit split.

positions.label: Civil deadline (30 days) applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, so the 30-day civil appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(a) applies.

positions.label: Criminal deadline (14 days) applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion is part of the criminal proceeding, so the 14-day criminal appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(b) applies.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in the equity of a debtor's asset belong to the bankruptcy estate or to the debtor upon good-faith conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether appreciation in property value between the petition date and conversion date inures to the bankruptcy estate or remains with the debtor. The Ninth Circuit held that such appreciation belongs to the estate, creating a split with circuits that hold the debtor retains the benefit of post-petition appreciation upon conversion.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the estate
positions.summary: Holds that the plain language of § 348(f)(1)(A), combined with § 541(a)'s broad definition of estate property, means post-petition appreciation in property value belongs to the bankruptcy estate upon conversion.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the debtor
positions.summary: Holds that § 348(f)(1)(A) was designed to protect good-faith converting debtors, and post-petition, pre-conversion appreciation in property value belongs to the debtor, not the estate.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Sentencing Guidelines when the state-controlled substance is not listed on the federal Controlled Substances Act schedules.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' requires the underlying substance to be federally scheduled, or whether any state-law drug offense qualifies regardless of federal scheduling. This has significant implications for base offense levels and career-offender designations.

positions.label: State offense qualifies regardless of federal scheduling
positions.summary: Holds that 'controlled substance offense' under U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2(b) broadly includes offenses under state law even if the particular substance is not controlled under the federal Controlled Substances Act.

positions.label: Substance must be federally scheduled
positions.summary: Holds that a state conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' only if the substance at issue is also controlled under the federal Controlled Substances Act.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: This case concerns when actuarial assumptions used to calculate employer withdrawal liability under ERISA must be finalized. The timing directly controls how much withdrawing employers must pay, affecting billions of dollars in potential obligations across thousands of employers participating in multiemployer pension plans.

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that the plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions after the statutory measurement date, as the statute does not require assumptions to be locked in by year-end.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that all actuarial assumptions must be established by the statutory measurement date to provide employers with predictability about potential withdrawal liability.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: GCIU-Employer Retirement Fund v. Goldfarb Corp.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated the conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether federal courts can apply a judicially-created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending the supervisory period beyond the time specified in the judgment when a person absconds. This affects sentencing calculations at revocation hearings for thousands of individuals who abscond annually.

positions.label: Tolling applies
positions.summary: Holds that supervised release is tolled during the period a supervisee absconds, extending the court's authority to revoke supervised release beyond the original term.

positions.label: No tolling without statutory authorization
positions.summary: Holds that courts lack authority to toll supervised release terms absent explicit statutory authorization, and the judicially-created fugitive tolling doctrine impermissibly extends punishment.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing motions under Section 2255.
splits.description: A 6-to-3 circuit split exists on whether federal prisoners face the categorical bar of § 2244(b)(1) — which prohibits raising any claim previously presented — in addition to the separate gatekeeping requirements of § 2255(h). If (b)(1) applies, federal prisoners are subject to a stricter standard than Congress may have intended for successive collateral attacks.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) applies to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that the § 2244(b)(1) bar on previously raised claims applies to federal prisoners' successive § 2255 motions, categorically barring claims that were raised in a prior motion.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1) does not apply to federal prisoners' § 2255 motions, meaning federal prisoners need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s requirements for successive motions.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether candidates can demonstrate Article III injury-in-fact sufficient to challenge election rules before an election takes place. The resolution affects the ability to bring pre-election challenges to voting procedures nationwide, with implications for mail-in voting rules, ballot counting deadlines, and election administration practices.

positions.label: Candidates have standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates for federal office have Article III standing to challenge election rules that may affect the counting of votes, based on competitive injury or vote-dilution theories.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

positions.label: Candidates lack standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates lack Article III standing for pre-election challenges because the alleged injury is speculative and contingent on future events.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: Bognet v. Secretary of Commonwealth of Pennsylvania

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: Whether an order denying a motion to seal documents containing private medical information is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine of Cohen v. Beneficial Industrial Loan Corp.
splits.description: The D.C. Circuit held that denial of a motion to seal medical records is immediately appealable as a collateral order because medical privacy is a value of 'high order.' Other circuits have taken different approaches to the collateral order doctrine's application to sealing orders, creating uncertainty about when interlocutory appeal is available for privacy-related sealing denials.

positions.label: Immediately appealable as collateral order
positions.summary: Holds that denial of a motion to seal medical records satisfies the collateral order doctrine because maintaining privacy in medical treatments and diagnoses is a value of high order that is effectively unreviewable after final judgment.

positions.label: Not immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that sealing denials generally do not satisfy the collateral order doctrine because the privacy interest, while significant, can be adequately vindicated through other means including protective orders or appeal after final judgment.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials, and whether Congress has constitutional power under the Spending Clause to impose such personal liability.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether RLUIPA permits suits for money damages against prison officials in their individual capacities. Some circuits allow such suits while others hold that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages, raising questions about the scope of Congressional spending power to impose personal liability on non-recipients of federal funds.

positions.label: RLUIPA allows individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA authorizes suits for money damages against state prison officials in their individual capacities, as the statute's text is broad enough to encompass such claims.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Landor v. Louisiana Dep't of Corrections

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials, and Spending Clause legislation cannot impose personal liability on individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether compassionate release motions may be used to raise claims that overlap with habeas corpus challenges, such as alleged sentencing errors or constitutional violations in the underlying conviction. Some circuits permit consideration of such factors, while others hold that § 3582(c)(1)(A) cannot be used as a substitute for § 2255 habeas relief.

positions.label: May consider conviction/sentence errors
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider legal errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as one factor in the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release.

positions.label: Cannot use compassionate release for habeas-type claims
positions.summary: Holds that § 3582(c)(1)(A) is not an alternative avenue for claims properly raised under § 2255, and errors in conviction or sentencing cannot constitute extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination or unfair treatment in the operation of hospitality or business establishments under federal civil rights law?
splits.description: The Supreme Court granted certiorari to resolve disagreement among circuits over the standards for discrimination claims against hospitality and business operators, including questions about liability and available remedies. The Second Circuit's approach was deemed sufficiently unsettled to warrant review.

positions.label: Broader liability standards
positions.summary: Holds that broader standards apply to discrimination claims against business establishments, potentially allowing for more expansive remedies.

positions.label: Narrower liability standards
positions.summary: Holds that narrower standards govern such claims, limiting the scope of liability and available remedies for discrimination in public accommodations.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which prohibits states from enacting laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any... broker,' preempts common-law negligence claims against freight brokers for injuries arising from the carrier's operations. This split affects the liability exposure of freight brokers nationwide.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are preempted by the FAAAA because they relate to the broker's services in arranging transportation.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are not preempted by the FAAAA because they are generally applicable common-law duties rather than regulations targeting broker services.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claim is based on the absence of a warning that the EPA did not require. The split affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticide products.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would effectively require labeling different from or in addition to what FIFRA and EPA regulations permit.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because such claims impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: DeKalb Genetics Corp. v. Bayer CropScience

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users.
splits.description: Following the Supreme Court's decision in Bruen, circuits have split on whether § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by users of controlled substances — particularly marijuana — is constitutional. Some circuits have upheld the law under historical tradition analysis, while others have found it unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by unlawful drug users is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation and survives Second Amendment scrutiny.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government has not demonstrated a historical tradition of disarming persons who use intoxicating substances.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the FAA's Section 1 transportation worker exemption, specifically whether workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of a broader interstate distribution chain are 'transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce.' The split affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a broad class of last-mile delivery workers.

positions.label: Broad interpretation — last-mile workers exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of an interstate distribution chain are transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow interpretation — last-mile workers not exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who merely distribute goods locally to retail stores are not transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce and remain subject to FAA arbitration agreements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
